description_full: Quanta Services, Inc. offers infrastructure solutions for the electric and gas utility, power generation, load center, manufacturing, communications, pipeline, and energy industries. The company's Electric Infrastructure Solutions segment engages in the design, procurement, construction, upgrade, repair, and maintenance of electric power transmission and distribution infrastructure and substation facilities; installation, maintenance, and upgrade of electric power infrastructure projects; installation of smart grid technologies on electric power networks; and design, installation, maintenance, and repair of commercial and industrial wirings. This segment offers aviation; emergency aerial firefighting services; emergency restoration; and other engineering and technical services; design and construction solutions to wireline and wireless communications, cable multi-system operators, technology companies, and other customers; engineering, procurement, new construction, and repair and maintenance services for renewable generation facilities; and training for electric workers, as well as training for the gas distribution and communications industries. Its Underground Utility and Infrastructure Solutions segment is involved in the transportation, distribution, storage, development, and processing of natural gas, oil, and other products, as well as owns and operates large load centers. This segment also engages in the design, engineering, procurement, construction, upgrade, and repair and maintenance services for natural gas systems; pipeline protection, integrity testing, rehabilitation, and replacement services; and catalyst replacement, high-pressure and critical-path turnaround, instrumentation and electrical, piping, fabrication, and storage tank services. The company was formerly known as Fabal Construction, Inc. and changed its name to Quanta Services, Inc. in November 1997. The company was incorporated in 1997 and is headquartered in Houston, Texas.

financial_summary: Quanta Services, Inc. is a large-cap industrials business with a $81.5B market cap on $28.5B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +19% over the past three years and +14% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.

Returns on capital run at 10% against a 10% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, and 15% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $1.6B in free cash flow — roughly 6 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.17× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.7× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 6.2×.
Shareholder yield is only 0.2%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Its 6% operating margin is roughly in line with the Industrials median (9%).
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.51x).

The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 544 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 63% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 24% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 31% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 49% and a beta of 1.11, it moves roughly with the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $638.7M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 42% in the 2020 crash, 22% in the 2022 bear market and 70% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $233 (margin of safety -133%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 62%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $149 to $356 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Industrials peers: P/E 49.0 vs 23.3, EV/EBITDA 22.5 vs 13.3 and P/FCF 50.3 vs 22.3 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 126% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 2.0% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 2.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The 29 covering analysts target $766 on average, 42% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 10% falls short of the cost of capital of 9.8%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have been steady (CV 0.24).
It runs a 15% gross margin and converts 6% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 2.17x.
ROE of 12% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.8x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.6% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.7x net debt to EBITDA ($439.5M of cash against $6.0B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 6.2x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 4.9, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 18.6% over 3 years, 20.5% over 5 years and 14.2% over 10 years.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 13.6% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.25 (orders outpacing sales), a backlog worth 83% of annual revenue and deferred revenue up 52%.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.5x, 2.1% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 26, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.7%), and institutions hold 92%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (27 sales, net $123.2M sold).
Shareholder yield is a modest 0.2% (0.2% in buybacks and 0.1% in dividends).
The share count has grown 1.1% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
people: With about 69,500 employees, each generates about $410K of revenue, in line with the Industrials median, and productivity has risen 14.4% a year.
That works out to $23K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $4.6M (11x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
